Knock-On

Measured attention, not proof of cause.

One trend. Where did the internet go next? Every right answer is a measured spike. Every wrong answer is a real page that stayed flat.

Methods & track recordArchiveProOpen data

Measured attention, not proof of cause. Every number is daily Wikipedia readers against the page's own 91-day baseline; wrong answers are real linked pages that stayed calm.

Sources: Wikimedia pageviews, links and clickstream (CC0 / open), Wikidata (CC0), Google Trends daily RSS (official feed), Bluesky trends (badge only), Google Trends "Trending Now" internal endpoint unofficial (free game only, never in open data). Clickstream data: not loaded yet.

Privacy: we store a hashed random ID, a daily-salted hash of your IP (for rate limits; the salt is deleted after the day), your picks and your country; no accounts. Waitlist emails are stored only for that list and can't be read back through the site.

By Ben Sunter · method v5.0

How to play

  1. Start at today's trending page. Each round shows four pages linked from the last one.
  2. One of them spiked after it. The other three are real linked pages whose readers stayed flat.
  3. Two tries a round: 🟩 first try, 🟨 second try, 🟥 missed (we show the answer and you carry on).
  4. Last, guess how big the final spike was. 2 points a round, up to 2 more for the guess.

Evidence labels

  • 📈 Spiked after / alongside daily readers rose past 3 robust deviations of the page's own baseline, the day of or after its parent.
  • 👣 Readers clicked through Wikipedia's monthly clickstream shows readers following that exact link.
  • 🎲 Fluke meter how often calm decoy pages pass the same test by chance.
  • 📱💻 Desktop and mobile the rise shows up on both.
  • Players' picks what other players chose, shown as players' picks from 30 players up. Never evidence.
  • AI-written context a caption written by Claude. It never adds hops or numbers.
